title: Node.js Export Authorization: Temporary User Downloads with Private Object Storage
author: SolomonFletcher5872
summary: The operational constraint is simple: an export link is a bearer credential, so it must outlive neither the user's need nor your authorization decision. Short answer: generate exports on the server, keep the bucket private, authorize the export in your application, and mint a short-lived signed download URL only after the file is ready. Start with a five-minute policy, then measure how long real clients take to begin downloads. That choice is different from putting a public URL in a job result. A signed URL limits exposure, but it does not identify the person using it. Anyone who obtains the link can use it until expiry. Your app still has to decide who may receive one. Five minutes. What should a Node.js SaaS flow check before signing an export? Treat the database row as the authorization record. A request should carry an opaque export ID, not a bucket and key selected by the browser. The Node.js handler authenticates the session, checks tenant and user ownership, confirms status == "ready" , and reads the object key stored with that record. Only then does it ask storage to sign a read. If generation is still running, return its job state; if it failed, return an application-level failure without exposing storage details. This ordering prevents a confused-deputy bug in the design: a valid user cannot persuade your signer to bless another tenant's key. It also fits notebook-to-prod work. A worker writes to an exports/ prefix, commits the row as ready after the write completes, and the web process creates a fresh link on demand. I would not put that URL in a durable email, analytics event, or model trace, and I don't cache it in a shared CDN. The query string is the credential. For a plain-HTTP provider such as Infrai, this signer can be called from a Node.js service without installing a storage SDK. One API contract works for any language that can send an HTTP request. The app remains the policy owner; the provider only creates the bounded read URL. Here is a minimal Python version of that provider call. The same request shape is straightforward to issue from Node.js with fetch ; I keep this example in Python because my eval harness runs beside the worker. import os import time import requests def presign_export ( bucket : str , key : str , expires_seconds : int = 300 ) -> str : api_key = os . environ [ " INFRAI_API_KEY " ] payload = { " op " : " get " , " expires_seconds " : expires_seconds } for attempt in range ( 4 ): response = requests . post ( f " https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/object/presign/ { bucket } / { key } " , headers = { " Authorization " : f " Bearer { api_key } " }, json = payload , timeout = 10 , ) if response . status_code == 429 : retry_after = response . headers . get ( " Retry-After " ) delay = float ( retry_after ) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt time . sleep ( delay ) continue response . raise_for_status () body = response . json () return body [ " url " ] raise RuntimeError ( " presign rate limit did not clear " ) Use the returned URL without adding the provider's Authorization header. Check the response body in your integration test and keep the bucket and key server-controlled. A presign operation is a read of policy state, so a retry does not create a second object; export creation itself should still use an application idempotency key. How do expiration, lifecycle cleanup, and export size fit together? Separate two clocks. URL expiry controls access to a ready object; lifecycle cleanup controls how long that object remains in storage. I usually test 60, 300, and 900 seconds as candidate link lifetimes, using the p95 time-to-first-byte and the slowest supported client as inputs. A mobile browser that suspends a tab changes the answer. Your mileage may vary. My eval checks invariants before it checks a vendor: an unauthorized caller gets no URL, a non-ready export gets no URL, the caller cannot choose the key, and the issued TTL stays within policy. Then I replay representative CSV and PDF sizes and record download-start latency. For example, I run the same export through a fast desktop connection, a throttled mobile profile, and a backgrounded browser tab; I record when the link is minted, when the first byte arrives, whether the user retries after a transient 429, and whether the object is deleted on schedule. A five-minute URL that works for a 2 MB CSV may be too short for a 900 MB archive, while a one-hour URL leaves a much larger bearer window when a support ticket includes the full address. This is more useful than a synthetic “URL works” test because it makes the expiry decision observable. Keep exports in a dedicated bucket or prefix so usage accounting and deletion rules are obvious. Lifecycle rules are a backstop, not a substitute for an application deletion deadline. The storage lifecycle minimum is one day, so it cannot enforce a 15-minute retention promise; delete sensitive artifacts from your worker or database-driven cleanup job as well. Multipart fragments also need an explicit cleanup plan. Which storage option fits a private export pipeline? The providers below all support private-object patterns, but their operational trade-offs differ. I would choose based on the rest of the system, not on a link-lifetime number. Option Good fit Trade-off to validate Amazon S3 Deep IAM, lifecycle, and multipart tooling More configuration and SDK surface across services Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible API with an edge-oriented deployment Check egress behavior and regional needs for your users Google Cloud Storage Teams already standardized on Google IAM and buckets A separate cloud's identity and network controls add work Infrai storage A mixed-language stack that wants one plain REST signer No public-read URLs, object versioning, object lock, or self-service CORS; vendor coverage is r2/s3/oss/cos rather than gcs/b2 Infrai is a reasonable fit when “no SDK to install” matters: a Python worker and a Node.js API can share an HTTP contract, with one key and billing surface for the platform's capabilities. It is not suitable for static website hosting, permanent public links, or a finance-grade immutable archive. There is no If-Match conditional write, cross-region automatic replication, or batch cross-cloud migration tool, so strict concurrency and disaster-recovery requirements belong in your database, queue, or an external storage design. Browser-direct upload is also a poor default for this export workflow. Bucket CORS rules are not self-service here, and exports are normally produced server-side anyway. If your product later accepts large user uploads, compare a server proxy with S3 multipart upload rather than assuming a single browser PUT will scale. A small launch checklist Before shipping, I want an authorization test for every tenant boundary, a ready-state test, and a check that logs redact the complete query string. I also want a refresh path: an authorized user can request a new URL without regenerating the export. Track issuance count, expiry-before-start rate, object age, and cleanup lag; those metrics tell you whether five minutes is conservative or wasteful. The catch is that a signed URL cannot revoke a copy already downloaded. For highly sensitive exports, shorten the TTL, add watermarking, or stream through an authenticated application endpoint. Stick with a provider that offers immutable retention and conditional writes when those are contractual requirements, even if its SDK is heavier. title: How We Built an Ultra-Lightweight Desktop AI Assistant (<35MB RAM) with Zero-DB RAG and Zero Bloat
author: GhostOS
summary: If you’ve tried running desktop AI assistants recently (LM Studio, Jan, AnythingLLM, Open-WebUI), you’ve probably noticed an infuriating trend: Most desktop AI tools consume 800MB to 1.4GB of RAM before you even load a single neural weight into memory. Why? Because almost every modern AI assistant is packaged as a bloated Electron container. When you finally load a 7B LLM (3GB VRAM), a vision model (2GB), and Whisper (1GB) for voice interaction, standard laptops and base 8GB Apple Silicon Macs instantly freeze or crash with brutal Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors. We asked a fundamental question: Can we build an autonomous, feature-packed desktop AI companion that idles at <35MB RAM, runs 100% offline, and never crashes an 8GB machine? That was the birth of GhostOS ( GitHub: GhostOS-ai/GhostOS ). Here is the engineering story of how we pulled it off. 1. Ditching Electron: The ~35MB RAM Native Architecture Electron bundles an entire Chromium browser and Node.js runtime for every single window. Instead of Electron, GhostOS uses OS-native web rendering engines : macOS: Apple WebKit Windows: Microsoft Edge WebView2 Linux: WebKitGTK The entire floating Casper mascot and Spotlight command bar (HUD) are rendered as transparent, frameless native webviews bridged directly to Python. Baseline Idle RAM Comparison: ┌─────────────────────────┬──────────────────┐ │ App │ Idle RAM (No LLM)│ ├─────────────────────────┼──────────────────┤ │ Jan / AnythingLLM │ ~850 MB – 1.2 GB │ │ LM Studio │ ~700 MB – 950 MB │ │ GhostOS (Native Engine) │ ~35 MB │ └─────────────────────────┴──────────────────┘ The difference is a 25x reduction in RAM footprint . Your CPU fans stay silent. 2. Dynamic VRAM Juggler: Solving the Multi-Model OOM Trap In an ideal workflow, you want: An LLM for reasoning and coding. A vision model for screen understanding. A speech model for voice input. If you keep all three resident in GPU VRAM, you need at least 6GB–8GB of pure VRAM , leaving nothing for macOS or Windows OS compositor. We implemented a Dynamic VRAM Juggler : The engine maintains a hot-swap memory scheduler. Models are unloaded to system cache and swapped into active GPU memory on-demand in <150ms . Peak VRAM is strictly capped at ≤3.5GB , making it rock-solid on budget PCs and 8GB MacBooks. 3. Zero-DB RAG: Document Chat Without Docker or Chroma Almost every RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) tutorial tells you to spin up Docker, install heavy vector databases (Chroma, Qdrant, Milvus), and download hundreds of megabytes of Python dependencies. For a desktop tool, that’s crazy overkill. We replaced the entire heavy vector stack with pure SQLite FTS5 (Full-Text Search 5) + BM25 ranking : Zero external database daemon. Zero network ports opened. Drag-and-drop any PDF, code file, or markdown note directly onto Casper. Document indexing happens in milliseconds with sub-millisecond retrieval latency. 4. 5 Killer Features That Elevate Productivity Ghostwriter (Global Clipboard AI): Select text anywhere — Slack, VS Code, Notes, Browser — hit your shortcut, and GhostOS rewrites, fixes grammar, or translates inline. Memory Vault: Cross-session persistent context graph stored in SQLite with zero VRAM overhead . GhostOS remembers your preferences and projects without wasting context tokens. Terminal Sandbox Lens: A proactive safety layer that intercepts dangerous commands ( rm -rf , DROP DATABASE , raw dd , format C: ) and explains the risks in plain English. Daily Standup & Commit Crafter: Analyzes your git diffs and terminal sessions to craft clean conventional commits and ready-to-share daily standup summaries. Auto-Minutes: Transcribes audio meetings and outputs an executive summary with actionable checklists. 5. 100% Paranoid Privacy Pledge No telemetry. No tracking. No phone-home pings. GhostOS operates completely air-gapped with Wi-Fi switched off. 🚀 Quickstart: Try It in 30 Seconds GhostOS is 100% open-source under the MIT license and published on PyPI. # Install globally via pip pip install ghostos-ai # Launch your floating Casper desktop companion ghost pet Or clone the repo: git clone https://github.com/GhostOS-ai/GhostOS.git cd GhostOS pip install -e . ghost pet GitHub Repository: https://github.com/GhostOS-ai/GhostOS PyPI Package: https://pypi.org/project/ghostos-ai Author: KIB.best (Contact: GhostOS@kib.best ) ⭐️ If you believe desktop software should be fast, lightweight, and private, give us a Star on GitHub! We'd love to hear your thoughts and benchmarks in the comments.

title: Five concepts to learn before you build with LLMs
author: Conor Bronsdon
summary: If you can ship ordinary software, you can start building with large language models. I would not start in the API console. I would learn five ideas in this order: machine learning, what an LLM is, generative AI versus older predictive AI, prompting, then evaluation. Each one has a small thing to try in code before you depend on a vendor SDK. What should I learn before I call a model? In traditional software, a programmer writes the rules. Machine learning works the other way: you show a model many examples, and a training process adjusts it until its predictions match those examples. The rules end up in learned parameters, not in a document you can read. Deep learning is the branch that uses neural networks with many layers, and it sits behind almost all recent AI progress. Large language models are deep learning models trained on text. The practical consequence is the same as for any machine learning system: the model is only as good as the data it learned from, and it can be confidently wrong on cases unlike its training data. What to try: encode the fraud-style rule from that definition ( amount over a threshold and a new country), then replace the rule with a weighted sum you chose by hand. You are not training a model. You are seeing that the "decision" is numbers, and those numbers only mean something relative to examples. What is an LLM actually doing? A large language model reads text as tokens and, given everything so far, predicts the next one. Repeat that and you get a paragraph. "Large" refers to the size of the neural network, measured in parameters, and to the amount of text it learns from in pre-training. Post-training then teaches it to follow instructions and hold a conversation. Because the model is built to produce plausible text, it can be fluent and wrong at the same time. On its own it also does not know about events after its knowledge cutoff, or about your private data. Most useful products wrap the model in more: retrieved documents, tools, memory, and checks. Dan Klein, co-founder and CTO of Scaled Cognition, argues that what people are using are plausibility engines: they assemble plausible outputs token by token. That is a strong way to get a prototype, and a weak way to get behavior you can guarantee. What to try: give yourself a four-word vocabulary and a function that returns the highest-scoring next token. Loop it ten times from a fixed prefix. Read the string you get and notice that nothing in the loop checked the sentence against a source of record. How is generative AI different from predictive AI? Much of the AI in business before 2022 was predictive: a model looked at an input and gave back a label or a number, such as fraud or not fraud, or a demand forecast. Generative AI produces something new instead: a paragraph, an image, a song, a block of code. Large language models generate text. Image, audio, and video models generate media, and multimodal models handle several of these at once. Generative AI and agentic AI are related but not the same. A generative model produces content when asked. An agent uses a generative model to plan and take actions toward a goal, calling tools and checking results along the way. I would get comfortable with the generator before I tried to build the agent. What to try: take one short support ticket and return two values from separate functions. One is a label, such as billing or access. The other is a drafted reply. The label is the older predictive job. The draft is the generative job. If you mix them in one return value, you will start treating a guess at a category as if it were a finished answer. What should I practice in the prompt? Prompt engineering is the craft of the instruction itself: how you phrase the task, what examples you include, what format you ask for, and how you structure the request. A clearer prompt produces better output. It is the first lever everyone reaches for, and it still matters. I would not treat clever wording as the place your system wins. As models got better at understanding intent, wording stopped being a durable advantage. It is table stakes. The work that used to hide inside slogans moved outward, to the documents, history, and tools you supply, and to what the system remembers across tasks. Learn the names later: context, and memory. Do the prompt exercises anyway. Then leave the thesaurus alone. Dan Klein's description of prompting as a control surface matches that limit. A prompt has no precise semantics and no guarantee. If the model ignores you, rewriting, capital letters, and extra exclamation points are weak recourse. What to try: one task, three prompts. A bare instruction. The same instruction plus one example. The same instruction plus a required format, such as one JSON object with two fields. Save all three outputs. You are practicing phrasing, examples, format, and structure, which is the whole craft named above. How do I know the answer is good enough to keep? Dan Klein argues that "how many of these scenarios did I get right" is the wrong shipping question. He wants to know, for how many scenarios, the system gets it right every time, including a hundred times in a row. A system at about 80% or 90% right is still, in his view, unshippable if one in ten customers is told a flight was booked when it was not. A system that gets 70% of scenarios right every single time is more valuable, because that is consistency you could put in a product. He also argues that putting a second model on top to check the first is a weak fix. Both can be wrong, and they tend to fail on the same hard cases, so in his estimate 80% checking 80% ends up around 82%. Add more checkers and the stack gets expensive and slow. Your first check can be smaller than a benchmark suite. Freeze the input. Run the call several times. Record whether the outputs agree, and whether they match a fact you already know. Fluency is not that check. On the reading list, the AI, decoded pages are grouped in five levels. If you are building, skim Level 1 (how a large language model works, why it costs what it costs, and why it makes things up), then Levels 4 and 5, where evaluation shows up as a builder's problem. After that, use Start here : five episodes on agents, evals, agent memory, AI infrastructure, and shipping AI in a real product. # Sketch for practice only. Not a client, and not a system any guest or lab runs. def rules_flag ( amount : float , new_country : bool ) -> bool : return amount > 1000 and new_country def learned_score ( amount : float , new_country : bool , w : tuple [ float , float ]) -> float : return w [ 0 ] * amount + w [ 1 ] * float ( new_country ) def next_token ( scores : dict [ str , float ]) -> str : return max ( scores , key = scores . get ) def draft_prompt ( task : str , example : str , fmt : str ) -> str : return f " Task: { task } \n Example: { example } \n Format: { fmt } " def same_every_time ( run , n : int = 5 ) -> bool : outs = [ run () for _ in range ( n )] return len ( set ( outs )) == 1 Checklist Treat machine learning as examples and parameters, and expect confident errors off that data. Read a paragraph as repeated next-token prediction, with hallucination, a knowledge cutoff, and no private data unless you supply it. Keep a predictive label and a generated draft in separate functions. Practice phrasing, one example, and a fixed format, then move on to context and memory. Repeat one frozen input and compare it to a known fact before you trust a single fluent answer. More on this topic, with the related episodes, is on Chain of Thought . title: Stop Letting Coding Agents Guess Call Chains: Tracing Blast Radius and Temporal Memory in FalkorDB
author: Nimit Sharma
summary: When you change a helper function in a backend service, ask an LLM coding assistant, it will likely do one of two things: retrieve the function name from a vector database, or extract a few top-k chunks from a vector database and guess. This is okay if the function is called directly from the test. It fails when your call chain is two or three hops long, or when an agent fails to find a solution to a problem today, saves the fact that it failed and moves on to tomorrow, when a commit alters the logic in the same module. I created GraphTriage ( github.com/Nimit15/GraphTriage ): an Incident resolution and session memory system supported by FalkorDB Cloud for WeMakeDevs × FalkorDB Graph Hacks 2026 (Track 1: Agents That Act on Connected Data, Track 2: Agent Memory and Coordination). GraphTriage is not a visualization supplement to the graph database, but rather it poses four specific questions using FalkorDB before an agent acts: Does the function or the test you are asking for exist in the graph? (If not, say NO right away rather than guess!) What is the exact call chain between the failed test and the broken function? What downstream functions and tests are contained within a blast radius of a change? Have we seen this fault signature before—and is that prior finding still ACTIVE , or has a newer commit marked it SUPERSEDED ? 1. The Graph Schema mapping in FalkorDB FalkorDB contains both repository (Track 1) and three-tier temporal memory (Track 2) data. Each workspace is separated at the database level using db.select_graph(f"graphtriage_ws_{workspace_id}") , to prevent memory leakage across tenants. graph LR M[":Module"] <-- DEFINED_IN --- F1[":Function (Caller)"] F1 -- CALLS --> F2[":Function (Callee)"] T[":Test"] -- COVERS --> F1 I[":EpisodicIncident"] -- IMPLICATES --> F2 SF_NEW[":SemanticFact (ACTIVE)] -- APPLIES_TO --> F2 SF_OLD[":SemanticFact (SUPERSEDED)]] PB[":ProceduralPlaybook"] -- REMEDIATES --> SF_NEW Nodes and Relationships Code Structure Nodes: ( :Module ) — pulled the source files from the repository. ( :Function ) — functions with module paths and line metadata, connected by [ :DEFINED_IN ] and directed [ :CALLS ] edges. ( :Test ) — test cases exercising the functions they cover via [ :COVERS ] edges. Three-Tier Memory Nodes: ( :EpisodicIncident ) – raw incident data (stack trace, failing test name, session id, timestamp). ( :SemanticFact ) — verified root-cause statements with temporal lifecycle properties ( valid_from , valid_to , status: ‘ACTIVE’ | ‘SUPERSEDED’ ) ( :ProceduralPlaybook ) - reusable remediation steps attached to recurrent fault signatures (e.g. KeyError: 'income' ), keeping track of usage_count over sessions. Figure 1. GraphTriage's local FalkorDB graph showing the code entities and relationships used for incident analysis. 2. Track 1: Explaining How the Graph Carries Out the Work (A Cypher That Contains No Text Written by a Large Language Model) A design rule that I adhered to right from the beginning was that the agent should never generate raw Cypher queries at runtime. Allowing an LLM to produce ad-hoc Cypher queries would lead to syntax errors and the invention of hallucinated edge labels. In order to avoid this, the agent interacts with FalkorDB only via the parameterized methods in src/core/incident_resolver.py and the fixed tools that are available through the official Model Context Protocol (MCP) SDK ( src/mcp/mcp_server.py ): trace_blast_radius find_failure_path run_targeted_tests Step 1: Refusing to Speculate on Unknown Entities Should you inquire of a typical RAG agent regarding a function that has been renamed or deleted, it will readily retrieve chunks of code that look similar and then fabricate an impact analysis. In the function IncidentResolver._validate_entity_existence() , each analysis begins with a parameterized check for existence in FalkorDB: def _validate_entity_existence ( self , entity_name : str ) -> bool : query = """ MATCH (n) WHERE (n:Function OR n:Test OR n:Module) AND n.name = $entity_name RETURN count(n) AS count """ result = self . graph . query ( query , { " entity_name " : entity_name }) return result . result_set [ 0 ][ 0 ] > 0 if result . result_set else False If FalkorDB returns 0 , analyze_impact() halts immediately and returns status: "UNVERIFIED_ENTITY" with hops: 0 and an explicit refusal reason: { "status" : "UNVERIFIED_ENTITY" , "hops" : 0 , "function_name" : "non_existent_helper" , "reason" : "Function 'non_existent_helper' not found in graph; refusing to speculate without graph evidence" , "affected_functions" : [], "impact_path" : [] } Every decision the agent makes is traceable back to graph state: if the node isn't in FalkorDB, the agent refuses to guess. Step 2: Tracing Real Bugs in sandbox_service To test GraphTriage end-to-end without mocks, sandbox_service/app.py models a multi-function service (7 functions and 12 tests) containing three intentional regressions: process_user_data : raises KeyError: 'income' when optional dictionary keys are missing. 2. calculate_growth_rate : uses bitwise XOR ( ^ ) instead of exponentiation ( ** ). 3. calculate_compound_interest : drops the exponent term in the compound formula. When test_incident_process_user_data_missing_income fails, GraphTriage queries the call chain ( [:COVERS] $\rightarrow$ [:CALLS] ) in FalkorDB to trace the path from the failing test to the underlying function, then computes the blast radius ( calculate_blast_radius ) using PageRank ( CALL algo.pageRank('Function', 'CALLS' ) with a < 2 node guard that falls back cleanly to direct relationship degree scoring). Instead of re-running all 12 tests in the sandbox on every edit, the agent queries FalkorDB for only the :Test nodes connected to the affected subgraph and executes pytest on that targeted subset. 3. Track 2: Multi-Agent Handoffs & Replacing Old Information When we store debugging history in a vector index that only adds new entries, old conclusions can stick around forever without anyone noticing. In the files src/core/multi_agent_pipeline.py and src/core/temporal_memory.py , the GraphTriage system manages three specific agents. These agents pass information between each other using a structured process called AgentHandoff , with FalkorDB storing the data: The TriageAgent looks at the stack trace, pulls out a standard signature for the error (like KeyError: 'income' ), records it as an EpisodicIncident, and then checks FalkorDB to see if there are any active SemanticFacts. 2. The BlastRadiusAgent takes the information from the TriageAgent, uses FalkorDB to find out how the failure spread and which functions were affected, and adds that graph evidence. 3. The MemoryCuratorAgent saves confirmed findings about the root cause as SemanticFact nodes and either finds or creates a ProceduralPlaybook. Marking Old Facts as Replaced with [:SUPERSEDED] Imagine a new code change affects how process_user_data handles default values. Instead of deleting the old SemanticFact (which would lose the debugging history) or just adding a new, conflicting fact, we use a function called supersede_fact() . This function sets an expiration date for the old fact, marks it as SUPERSEDED , and connects the new fact to the old one: # Initial architectural finding saved in Session 1 memory . create_semantic_fact ({ " statement " : " process_user_data should use user.get( ' income ' , 0) " , " valid_from " : " 2026-10-17T10:00:00Z " , " status " : " ACTIVE " }) # Superseded after schema update in Session 2 memory . supersede_fact ( old_fact_id , { " statement " : " process_user_data validates schema via default dict mapping " , " valid_from " : " 2026-10-18T14:00:00Z " , " status " : " ACTIVE " }) In Cypher, closing the old fact while preserving the lineage looks like this: MATCH ( old: SemanticFact { fact_id: $old_fact_id }) SET old.valid_to = $timestamp , old.status = 'SUPERSEDED' CREATE ( new: SemanticFact { fact_id: $new_fact_id , statement: $statement , valid_from: $timestamp , valid_to: null , status: 'ACTIVE' }) - [ :SUPERSEDED ] -> ( old ) When a future session queries memory, the fast retrieval path filters strictly on status = 'ACTIVE' AND valid_to IS NULL . The agent gets only current truth in its context window, while the [:SUPERSEDED] chain preserves the full audit trail. Figure 2. GraphTriage's incident-resolver and temporal-memory tests running against a local FalkorDB instance (19 passed). 4. Engineering Lessons From Setting Up FalkorDB Cloud When I built and tested this on Windows with a live FalkorDB Cloud , I learned some practical things: 1. Centralizing Cloud Connection and Default Parameter Issues ( src/core/db_connection.py ) : At first, having default host="localhost" in our class constructors would quietly ignore the .env variables when setting up test data. We fixed this by putting all connection code into one place ( db_connection.py ). This setup loads .env variables and allows overriding them, splits the host and port, and has a fallback for SSL. Now, switching between our local Docker setup ( localhost:6379 ) and FalkorDB Cloud is easy. 2. MCP Server Startup and Module Name Conflicts: We named our local folder src/mcp/ , but this conflicted with the official mcp package we installed through pip. This happened when we set PYTHONPATH=/app/src in Docker. By changing to import from the project root (using PYTHONPATH=/app and running commands like python -m src.mcp.mcp_server ) and giving InitializationOptions() to mcp_server.run() , we fixed the startup problems. 2. Comparing Step-by-Step Path Finding vs. Wildcard Shortest Path: In OpenCypher, how patterns with unbounded or undirected paths work can be different on various graph databases compared to Neo4j. We used specific directed relationships (like [:COVERS] and [:CALLS] ) along with checking the call chain step-by-step and using a fallback based on how connected a node is. This made our path tracing completely predictable in all 8 integration tests. All tests passed , with one warning , and it took 10.49 seconds against the live FalkorDB Cloud. 5. Current Limitations & Next Steps Language Parser Scope: The system currently takes in Python modules and follows pytest conventions; the next logical step is to expand the AST loader to support TypeScript and Go using Tree-sitter. Containerized Test Runner: The current test execution runs in a subprocess with a time limit; putting test runs inside containers would make it more reliable for use in multi-user CI pipelines. title: SEO Health Basics for Personal Websites and Portfolios
author: Sandeep Singh
summary:
A personal website does a specific job. When a recruiter, client, conference organiser or potential collaborator searches your name, it should come up, look professional and lead them to your best work. You don't need to rank for competitive keywords. You need to be findable for your name and your niche , and you need the site to work when someone arrives. That second part gets overlooked. Portfolios are built once, often in a weekend, and then left alone for years while the things they link to change underneath them: demo apps on free hosting tiers get shut down, repos get renamed or archived, client sites get redesigned, conference talk pages disappear. The person reviewing your work doesn't know any of that. They just see a broken link next to your name. This guide is a health check, not a growth hack. It covers what to set up once, and what to check regularly so the site keeps doing its job. Part 1: Can Google find and index your site? Verify in Search Console Add your site to Google Search Console . It's free, and it's the only direct source of truth about how Google sees your site. After verification: Use URL Inspection on your homepage. It tells you whether the page is indexed and, if not, why. Check Indexing â†’ Pages for pages excluded by noindex , redirects or errors. Check you haven't hidden the site by accident A common portfolio problem is a noindex left over from development, or a theme setting like WordPress's "Discourage search engines from indexing this site" left ticked. Google's documentation is explicit: when it finds the noindex rule, it will "drop that page entirely from Google Search results, regardless of whether other sites link to it" ( Block Search indexing with noindex ). View the page source and search for noindex , and check response headers for X-Robots-Tag : curl -sI https://yourname.dev | grep -i x-robots-tag Also check robots.txt isn't blocking everything ( Disallow: / ). Note that the same Google page warns that if robots.txt blocks a page, Google can't see its noindex rule at all, so don't combine the two. Do you need a sitemap? Probably not urgently. Google says you might not need a sitemap if your site is "small", about 500 pages or fewer, and comprehensively linked internally ( Sitemaps overview ). Most portfolios qualify. If your static site generator or CMS produces one automatically, though, submitting it in Search Console doesn't hurt. Part 2: Make your links crawlable This one catches a lot of developer portfolios, especially single-page apps. Google's link guidance says that, generally, Google "can only crawl your link if it's an HTML element ... with an href attribute", and that most other formats won't be parsed ( Link best practices ). So if your navigation is built from
or Most frameworks' router link components ( in Next.js, in Vue, and so on) render a real , so use those rather than click handlers. A quick check: disable JavaScript in your browser and see whether you can still navigate. Part 3: Titles and descriptions Page titles The is usually the clickable headline in search results. Google's guidance asks for titles that are descriptive and concise, unique to each page, and free of keyword stuffing ( Title links ). For a portfolio: Homepage: Ana Rivera, Frontend Developer in Lisbon Project page: Weather App (React, Mapbox) | Ana Rivera Blog post: the post's actual title, plus your name if it fits The commonest problem on portfolios is every page sharing the same title, like "Portfolio" or "Home", because the template was never changed. Meta descriptions Google says snippets are primarily created from the page content, but it "sometimes uses the meta description HTML element if it might give users a more accurate description of the page" ( Snippets ). Write a unique, plain-English description for at least the homepage and key projects. One or two sentences on who you are, what you do and what's on the page is enough. Duplicate URLs If your site responds on both www and non- www , or on both http and https , pick one version and redirect the others to it with a single 301. You can also add a rel="canonical" tag pointing at the preferred URL. Google treats canonical tags as a strong signal for choosing which duplicate to show, but not as a guarantee ( Consolidate duplicate URLs ). Part 4: The links that actually matter, to your work Here's where personal sites lose the most value. A portfolio is a set of claims ("I built this", "I spoke here", "I wrote this") backed by links. When the links die, the claims look unverifiable. Link rot is not a fringe problem. Pew Research Center found that 38% of webpages that existed in 2013 were no longer accessible a decade later, and even of pages collected in 2021, about one in five were gone two years later ( Pew Research Center, 2024 ). A portfolio that links out to many projects, employers and talks is exposed to all of that. Common culprits: Live demos on free hosting tiers that sleep, expire or were deleted when you cleaned up your account GitHub repos that were renamed, made private or moved to an organisation (GitHub redirects renamed repos, but not deleted or private ones) Client and employer sites that were redesigned, so the specific page you built no longer exists Talks and articles on event or publication sites that reorganised their archives Your own old URLs after you moved from one static site generator or host to another How to check Crawl your own site with Screaming Frog SEO Spider (free for up to 500 URLs; limits ). Enable external link checking, then look at Response Codes â†’ Client Error (4xx) and Server Error (5xx) , and use Inlinks to find which page holds each broken link. Or script it. For a small site, a short script that pulls every href and requests each one is a fine weekend exercise. Treat timeouts and 5xx errors as "check again later" rather than definitely broken. Look past status codes. A deleted demo on some hosts returns a 200 with a generic "app not found" page. Open your most important links by hand now and then. How to fix Update the link to the new location. For a dead demo, replace it with a short screen recording or screenshots, and say the live version is offline. For a deleted article or talk page, link to an archived copy in the Wayback Machine if one exists. If you changed your own URL structure, redirect old paths to the new ones so links from other people's sites keep working. Part 5: Images, HTTPS and speed Images Portfolios are image-heavy, and missing images are the most visible kind of breakage: a gallery of broken-image icons. After any move or rebuild, check every project page. For the images that work, add meaningful alt text. Google calls alt text "the most important attribute when it comes to providing more metadata for an image", and it also helps people using screen readers ( Image SEO best practices ). HTTPS and mixed content Serve everything over HTTPS. If an HTTPS page loads assets over plain HTTP, browsers treat that as mixed content. Some images, video and audio are automatically upgraded to HTTPS, and scripts, stylesheets and iframes are blocked outright ( MDN: Mixed content ). Old embeds and hard-coded http:// image URLs are the usual cause. Search your source for http:// . Speed Run your homepage and a heavy project page through PageSpeed Insights or Lighthouse in Chrome DevTools. On portfolios the big wins are almost always oversized images (export at display size, use modern formats) and unnecessary third-party scripts. Part 6: A maintenance routine that fits a side project You won't audit your personal site every week, and you don't need to. A light routine: After every change (deploy, redesign, host move): Click through every page with JavaScript disabled Check for noindex and robots.txt surprises Confirm old URLs redirect in one hop Monthly (10 minutes): Glance at Search Console for new errors Open your three most important project links by hand Quarterly: Full crawl with external link checking Fix or replace dead demos, repos and article links Update titles and descriptions if your role or focus has changed Automate what's tedious. Link and image checks are the part that's easy to forget and easy for software to do. An automated daily check means a demo that dies the week before you apply for a job shows up as an email, not as a recruiter's silent impression. Disclosure: I build Uchik, a tool for that last step. Uchik crawls your site every day and emails a short report of broken internal and external links, missing images, redirect chains, HTTPS problems and basic SEO gaps such as missing titles, meta descriptions and canonical tags, each with the page and HTML element to fix. The features page lists the checks, and the FAQ covers what it does and doesn't do. One limit is relevant here: links that only exist after JavaScript runs may be missed, which is one more reason to use real <a href> links. You can sign up for free , no credit card needed. Screaming Frog's free tier and a quarterly reminder in your calendar also work. Quick checklist [ ] Site verified in Search Console; homepage indexed [ ] No stray noindex , X-Robots-Tag or Disallow: / [ ] Navigation uses real <a href> links [ ] Unique, descriptive <title> on every page [ ] Meta descriptions on homepage and key projects [ ] One canonical version of the domain (HTTPS, www or not) [ ] No broken links to demos, repos, employers, talks or articles [ ] No missing images; alt text on project images [ ] No mixed content [ ] Routine scheduled or automated Your personal site is often the first piece of your work someone sees. Keeping it findable and unbroken is a small, regular job, and it's worth it.

title: How to prove an online JWT tool isn’t stealing your token

summary: Most free JWT decoders ask you to paste a token. That’s a trust problem. Tokens can include emails, roles, and session data.
