title: How to Find and Fix Broken Links on a Shopify Store
author: Sandeep Singh
summary: A broken link on a store costs more than one on a blog. A dead link in a blog post loses a reader. A dead link in your main menu, in a "Shop the look" block or on a cart upsell loses an order, and Shopify won't tell you about it. Products get deleted, collections get renamed, apps get uninstalled, themes get swapped, and every one of those changes can leave behind links that now lead to "Page not found." This guide shows a repeatable way to find those links with free tools and fix them properly. You don't need a developer or a paid app. Where broken links come from on Shopify Knowing the usual causes tells you where to look first: Deleted or drafted products. A product that is deleted, set to Draft or removed from the Online Store channel returns a 404. Every link to it from a collection description, blog post, menu or "related products" block now breaks. Changed URL handles. If you rename a product or collection and edit its handle, the old URL stops working unless a redirect was created. Menu items pointing at things that no longer exist. Menus (Content â†’ Menus in the Shopify admin) often link to seasonal collections or pages that were removed months ago. Hard-coded links in theme sections and rich text. Banners, slideshows and "image with text" blocks often have full URLs pasted in by hand. Typos and old handles hide here. External links. Links to suppliers, size guides on other sites, social profiles or affiliate partners break when their sites change. Images. An image deleted from Files, or a hot-linked image on another server, leaves an empty box where a product photo should be. Step 1: Check what Google has already found (Google Search Console) If you haven't connected Google Search Console yet, verify your domain and submit your sitemap ( yourstore.com/sitemap.xml ; Shopify generates it automatically). Then open Indexing â†’ Pages and look under "Why pages aren't indexed" for: Not found (404). URLs Google tried to crawl that no longer exist. Redirect error. Redirects that loop or go nowhere. Click into each list to see example URLs. The URL Inspection tool tells you where Google first discovered a URL, which often points to the page holding the bad link. Know the limits. Google crawls on its own schedule, so the report lags behind your changes. It only shows URLs Google cares to crawl, so it won't list a broken link in your footer if Google hasn't recrawled that page yet. And a 404 isn't always a problem: Google's documentation says URLs that return 4xx codes are dropped from the index over time ( Google: how HTTP status codes affect crawling ). That's fine for a product you truly retired. What you need to fix are the links that still point to it. Step 2: Crawl your own store A crawler visits your pages the way a visitor would and reports every link that returns an error, along with the page that contains it. That second part is what makes it useful. Free options: Screaming Frog SEO Spider (free version). A desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux. The free version crawls up to 500 URLs per crawl, which covers many small stores. Saving crawls and most advanced settings need the paid licence ( Screaming Frog pricing and limits ). After a crawl, filter Response Codes â†’ Client Error (4xx) , select a URL, and open the Inlinks tab at the bottom to see every page that links to it, with the anchor text. Free online checkers such as Dead Link Checker or W3C's Link Checker are fine for a quick look at a small site. They usually report less about where the link lives. Tips for crawling a Shopify store: Start from your homepage and let the crawler follow internal links. Your main navigation and footer are on every page, so a broken menu link shows up on every page of the report. Fix it once and the whole list shrinks. Exclude URLs you don't care about: /cart , /account , /search? and filter or sort parameters such as ?sort_by= and ?filter. . Those create many near-duplicate URLs and eat your 500-URL allowance. Crawl gently. Most desktop crawlers let you limit requests per second. One or two is plenty for a small store. Crawl after every big change: a theme switch, a bulk product import, an app removal or a menu rebuild. Step 3: Check the pages that make money, by hand Crawlers follow links in the HTML. Some Shopify themes and apps inject buttons, upsells or recommendations with JavaScript, and crawlers that read only server HTML can miss them. So once a month, walk the purchase path yourself: Open your homepage in a private window. Click each main menu item and each homepage banner. Open a best-selling product, add it to the cart, and continue to the checkout page. Stop before paying. Open the browser developer tools (F12) â†’ Network tab, reload, and sort by Status . Anything red (404, 500) is a resource or link that failed. Do the same on your phone. Mobile menus are often separate markup. This takes about ten minutes and catches problems no crawler sees. Step 4: Fix each broken link the right way For each broken URL you'll make one of three fixes. Fix A: Update the link at its source (best) If the link is under your control (a menu item, a banner, a product description), edit it to point straight at the right live URL. A direct link is always better than a link that relies on a redirect. Menus: Content â†’ Menus â†’ open the menu â†’ click the broken item â†’ choose the new collection, product or page. Theme sections: Online Store â†’ Themes â†’ Customize â†’ find the section â†’ update the link field. Rich text (descriptions, pages, blog posts): open the item, select the link, and edit it. Switch to the HTML view ( <> ) if the link is buried. Fix B: Add a URL redirect (for URLs other people link to) If the old URL is in emails, ads, social posts or other sites' backlinks, you can't edit those links. Add a 301 redirect so visitors land somewhere useful: Go to Content â†’ Menus â†’ View URL redirects â†’ Create URL redirect . In Redirect from , enter the old path (e.g. /products/blue-summer-dress ). In Redirect to , enter the closest live match: the replacement product, or the parent collection. Avoid sending everything to the homepage; it frustrates visitors. A few Shopify rules worth knowing, all from Shopify's URL redirect documentation : A redirect only works if the "from" URL is actually broken. If a page still loads there, the redirect is ignored. You can't redirect from reserved paths such as /cart , /orders or /apps . When you hide a product or collection, then redirect its URL, and later make it visible again, Shopify deletes that redirect automatically. Redirects can be exported and imported as CSV. That's handy for bulk fixes after a migration. When you change a product or collection handle in the "Search engine listing" section, Shopify offers to create the redirect for you. Leave that box ticked. Fix C: Remove the link If the destination is gone for good and there is no sensible replacement (an expired partner offer, a discontinued external guide), remove the link or replace it with plain text. Step 5: Fix external links and images External links: open each one. If the page has moved, update to the new URL. If it's gone, link to a different source or remove it. For affiliate links, check that the link still goes to the right product, not just that it loads. Images: in the crawler, filter by images with a 4xx response. Re-upload missing images to Content â†’ Files and update the reference. Don't hot-link images from other domains; when those servers change, your images break. Step 6: Prevent the next batch Most broken links are created during routine admin work, so a few habits prevent most of them: Before deleting a product, search your store admin and theme for its handle, and decide where its URL should redirect. Keep the redirect box ticked whenever you edit a handle. Use relative links ( /collections/sale ) in theme settings instead of full URLs. They survive domain changes. After uninstalling an app, check the pages where it showed widgets. Leftover blocks or snippets can point to app URLs that no longer exist. Re-crawl on a schedule. Monthly for small stores, weekly if you publish or change products often. Automating the check The manual routine works, but it relies on you remembering to run it, and a broken link created on Tuesday can sit there for weeks. If you'd rather have it run on its own, there are scheduled options: Screaming Frog's paid licence can schedule crawls, several Shopify apps monitor 404s, and hosted crawlers will email you results. Disclosure: I build Uchik, a hosted option of this kind. Uchik crawls a store daily with read-only GET requests and emails a list of broken links, missing images and redirect problems. The features page lists every check it runs, and each issue comes with the page and the exact HTML tag that caused it, as you can see in this sample ecommerce report . You can sign up for free , no credit card needed. It reads server-delivered HTML ( the FAQ explains what that means for JavaScript-added links), so the manual checkout walk-through in Step 3 is still worth doing. Quick checklist [ ] Search Console connected, sitemap submitted [ ] Indexing â†’ Pages â†’ "Not found (404)" reviewed [ ] Store crawled with cart, account and filter URLs excluded [ ] Every 4xx link traced to its source page via Inlinks [ ] Links fixed at source; redirects added for externally shared URLs [ ] Purchase path walked by hand on desktop and mobile [ ] Next crawl date in the calendar Broken links rarely appear all at once. They pile up one admin change at a time, and a short, regular check is the easiest way to keep them under control.

title: Black Box: finding yesterday's warning signs in 225,000 maintenance reports
author: Divyam Singh
summary: On 1 April 2011, Southwest Flight 812 lost a five-foot strip of fuselage skin at 34,000 feet. Everyone survived. The NTSB's final report described fatigue cracks along one lap joint, stringer S-4L. Here's the part that keeps you up at night: mechanics had filed reports about cracked clips on that exact stringer before the accident. Two of them, on the same tail number, twenty-four inches from where the roof later tore. Nobody reads those records together. The investigation lives in one database, the maintenance paperwork lives in another, and the person who could act on the pattern is a structures engineer with a queue full of work orders. The datasets aren't secret. They're just apart. That's the bet behind Black Box , our project for the FalkorDB Graph Hacks hackathon: this is a graph problem. If maintenance reports, NTSB findings, and FAA airworthiness directives all live in one graph that understands where on the aircraft a report points, then the precursor pattern shows up as a query, not a coincidence. One graph, two filing cabinets We ingested two public datasets into a single FalkorDB graph — NTSB accident reports and FAA maintenance reports, ~225,000 records — plus the FAA's Airworthiness Directives, the official "fix this" mandates, and, in a later pass the same week, the actual text of those directive documents and the NTSB brief themselves, sectioned and dated. The core design decision is an address system for parts of an aircraft . Every report attaches to a Location node that refines in three steps: a zone — fuselage section 53, the lower skin a line — stringer S-4L, one specific structure inside it a bin — a 20-inch stretch of that stringer: the literal segment where the failure happened Two datasets that never knew about each other now meet at the same address, down to the foot. A "find the warning sign" question stops being an analytics project and becomes one walk of the graph: // Reports on one tail , at one address , before the clock we 're standing at MATCH (r:Report)-[:ON]->(:Aircraft {tail:' N648SW '}), (r)-[:AT]->(:Location)-[:WITHIN*0..2]->(line:Location {level:' line '}) WHERE r.date < $asOf RETURN r.id, r.date, r.text For followers of this case, the output of the fleet version of that query is the famous number: Southwest 737 Classics reporting skin cracks on stringer 4 went 9 → 18 → 31 between 2008 and 2010, three months before the accident. And it wasn't the loudest line overall — other stringers had more total reports. What stood out was the rise : second of 37 lines on our checked date. A lead worth review, not a prediction. The time machine Every investigation in the app carries a date, and the graph obeys it. Set the clock to 31 March 2011 and the NTSB's report about the accident is not there . Documents dated after the cutoff are invisible, down to the emergency AD issued five days after the accident. Why so strict? Because most "we saw it coming" demos cheat without meaning to: the accident's own report leaks into the evidence pool, or the model quietly reads documents published afterwards. Ours is overfitting-resistant by construction — the rule is a date clamp on the graph, not a narrative. And because one memorable example is a trap, we built a backtest harness and ran our naive lead-signal across every NTSB event that had earlier reports. It initially scored three times better than chance. Then we closed two leaks — the accident's own report in scope, and aircraft families that always report the same systems — and the advantage fell to 0.9, no better than chance . A system-level match is not a warning sign. What mattered was the exact location and the fleet trend. That negative result is the honest center of this project, and the app shows it. The agent: useful, but on a leash The investigation board hosts an AI agent (a free-tier model on OpenRouter) that investigates through an MCP server we expose over the graph. The agent picks which tool to call next and writes the conclusions. Every one of those tools is a fixed Cypher query — the model never writes a query; it chooses among queries we wrote and verified, so a hallucination can't become a fake datapoint. Two deliberate guardrails: There is no approve tool on the agent's server. If its evidence is strong, it may draft a failure mode — linked to the reports and accident that support it, status proposed . Only a person can confirm, defer, or merge it, in the UI. When our agent's first live answer drifted into causal language ("this caused the failure"), our harness made it rewrite. We surface warning signs, never causes. A lead is a lead. Human decisions get routed like real decisions. A confirmed risk becomes an alert, then a work-order draft — routed to the team that owns that ATA chapter, and to a specific engineer picked by who worked that exact line before the investigation date , with the fewest open jobs. The graph ends where responsibility begins. The third layer of rigor is the paper trail itself: the AD paragraphs and the NTSB brief live in the graph as dated sections, linked to the locations they concern, so "the records said this" can be checked against the paper it came from — while still respecting the date clamp. What we learned shipping it Model the address, not the abstraction. The best decision we made was treating "where on the aircraft" as a sharp, ladder-shaped property (zone → line → bin) instead of free text. Everything else — heat maps, trends, documents, agent tools — slotted into that shape. Graph queries read like the domain. Our judge-facing pitch is one Cypher query, not an architecture diagram: reports ON a tail, AT a location, WITHIN a stringer, before a date. A date clamped graph is a cheap honesty engine. One WHERE r.date < $asOf everywhere beat any amount of prompt engineering about "don't use future knowledge". Deployment is where the war stories live. The whole stack — FalkorDB v4.14.6 plus a Next.js app — runs as one warm container on Modal, with the graph shipped as a 63 MB RDB in a volume, cold boot under a minute. Which sounds smooth now. It took two genuinely fun bugs to get there: the database image's own startup script quietly hijacked container boot (running its bundled Redis and a browser UI instead of our code), so Modal kept killing "initializing" containers — fixed by blanking the image's ENTRYPOINT; and Modal refusing to mount a volume over a path the image has files baked into — fixed by moving the mount. Everything was our own Docker-free setup flowing through docker compose locally first, which is why none of this showed up until the first deploy.

title: The bug is in the arrangement: finding and cutting your AI agent's data-leak paths
author: Bhanu Nagpure
summary: Give an agent three ordinary tools: one that reads a GitHub issue, one that reads a local folder, one that can post a GitHub comment. Each behaves exactly as documented. Each is useful on its own. Together they form an exfiltration path — an instruction hidden in the issue can steer the agent into reading the folder and publishing it to a public repository. Security researchers have a name for the setup: Simon Willison's lethal trifecta — read untrusted input, touch private data, write somewhere public. What made me build something about it is how little malice the leak actually needs. In MCPHunt , a controlled benchmark of multi-server MCP agents, policy-violating credential propagation appeared in 11.5–41.3% of runs depending on the model — when the task allowed redacting the credential. No attacker required. The arrangement alone did it. That is the uncomfortable property of this bug class: every component is correct. The bug is the composition — and a composition of tools and data is a path. Paths and cuts are what graphs answer, so I built LethalPath : it reads a Claude Desktop-style MCP config, models the tools, the data they touch and the agent's shared context as a graph in FalkorDB, finds the leak routes, computes a minimum cut of permissions to revoke, and then proves the fix by re-running the query. The model: small enough to read in one sitting The whole schema fits in a table: Node Holds Server which MCP server supplies which tools Tool name, server, how the label was derived Resource data, by label only: kind, scope, trust, sensitivity, visibility Context one hub per agent — the window one tool's output enters and another tool reads from Meta config counts and a ready flag, the last write of ingest One relationship carries the weight: ( a ) - [ :FLOWS { dir: 'feeds' | 'emits' , capacity , revocable , grant , taskCost }] -> ( b ) Two decisions worth explaining. One relationship type, because algo.maxFlow on FalkorDB 6.0.2 accepts exactly one — my planned FEEDS / EMITS pair collapsed into FLOWS with a dir property, and the schema ended up simpler than the plan. And capacity encodes cost, not volume : a grant with a declared task behind it costs more to cut, so the cut prefers revoking permissions that nothing depends on. The query a join cannot write The leak has a shape: untrusted input reaches the shared context through one tool, and a private store reaches a public sink through a chain that passes through the same context. MATCH inj = ( u: Resource { trust: 'untrusted' }) - [ :FLOWS ] -> ( :Tool ) - [ :FLOWS ] -> ( ctx: Context ) MATCH leak = ( p: Resource { sensitivity: 'private' }) - [ :FLOWS * 1 .. 5 ] -> ( ctx ) - [ :FLOWS * 1 .. 5 ] -> ( s: Resource { visibility: 'public' }) RETURN u.kind AS injected_from , [ n IN nodes ( leak ) WHERE n: Tool | n.name ] AS tools , length ( leak ) AS hops ORDER BY hops ASC LIMIT 25 Two things matter more than they look. First: "through the same context" is the entire bug class. A join over permissions tells you a tool can read and a tool can write. It does not tell you that one tool's output lands exactly where the next tool picks it up. A per-server scanner sees a read here and a write there; the laundering hop in the middle is invisible to it. A vector index can rank tools by similarity; it cannot answer reachability through a hub. Second: the walk is anchored and bounded. My first version let the path wander ( *2..10 ); a twelve-tool config timed the server out, because the walk re-enters the shared hub exponentially. Bounding each segment at five hops and anchoring both on the tainted context fixed the performance and tightened the semantics — the route must pass through that context itself. On a 40-tool config that chains through the hub, the walk count is still enormous (126,321), so the CLI catches the failure and retries with a query that counts without materialising paths, marking the order as arbitrary so nothing downstream mistakes arbitrary for shortest. The cut is unaffected. The fix: one call — and the cut is yours Private stores are sources; public sinks are targets: CALL algo.maxFlow ({ sourceNodes: src , targetNodes: dst , relationshipTypes: [ 'FLOWS' ], capacityProperty: 'capacity' }) YIELD maxFlow , edges , edgeFlows Here is the part I did not expect: algo.maxFlow returns flows, not a cut. A maximum flow admits two canonical minimum cuts — one hugged to the sources, one to the sinks. Both close every route; they revoke different permissions and break different declared tasks. LethalPath walks the residual graph in its own code, compares both canonical cuts, and picks the cheaper one: fewer distinct grants first, fewer broken declared tasks second, and on a full tie, the write side — so the agent keeps its ability to read and loses only the publish. That cut-selection code is the most product-shaped part of the repo, and it exists only because the engine didn't do it for me. I am glad it ended up in my code instead of hidden behind a yield. The receipt The fix ends by re-running the leak query with the revoked grants excluded: WHERE all ( rel IN relationships ( leak ) WHERE rel.grant IS NULL OR NOT ( rel.grant IN $revoked )) RETURN count ( leak ) AS remaining Zero rows is the receipt. Not "should be fixed" — the same query that found the leak, finding nothing. The numbers, each with the file that contains it (a rule the repo follows everywhere): 40/40 detection and 40/40 fix-quality across 40 seeded configs (16 planted leaks, 8 laundering-only, 8 clean, 8 tie cases; seed committed). The 8 clean configs return an empty cut and the tool stays silent on them. A config built from the official MCP server READMEs: 567 routes closed by 9 revocations ; the re-run finds 0 of 567 . The 40-tool hub config: 126,321 routes → one grant → 0 of 126,321. Limits, stated as plainly as the numbers: the eval is synthetic (my generator), so it shows the engine is consistent with its spec, not that it is right about your setup. Labels are inferred from tool names, not verified against server code. The traversal is bounded at five hops per segment. The runtime guard is a demo with simulated tool results — real MCP stdio, no real GitHub or filesystem behind it yet. None of that goes on a slide as more than it is. What I learned The docs were ahead of the engine. FalkorDB's shortest-path index (CCH) is documented; on the pinned 6.0.2 image both CREATE CCH INDEX and db.idx.cch.query fail. I planned around a feature that does not ship, and un-planned it into algo.SPpaths / algo.SSpaths fallbacks with a maxLen bound. The lesson: verify every load-bearing claim by execution, and commit the fallback next to the claim. A constraint made the design better. One relationship type wasn't a compromise; it forced the model to carry direction as data and ended up readable. Refusal order beats sanitising. Every product read goes through GRAPH.RO_QUERY with a 3-second timeout, a LIMIT cap, and write keywords refused before dispatch. The server rejects instead of negotiating, and the guard follows the same shape — block first, then log the tool, the decision, the reason, and a hash of the arguments. Never the arguments. The weakest part is the labelling, and it is worth saying so. MCP tools don't declare their trust level; we infer it from names with a conservative fallback for anything the rules can't classify. Mislabel a tool and the route set changes. It is on the site, in the README, and in the tool's own limits section. Try it Everything runs locally — Docker + pnpm, no model call, no API key, no telemetry: git clone https://github.com/bhanu-dev82/lethalpath && cd lethalpath docker compose up -d && pnpm install && pnpm build node packages/cli/dist/index.js scan --mcp your-mcp-config.json Code: https://github.com/bhanu-dev82/lethalpath Site: https://www.devanshustudios.com/lethalpath/ Walkthrough (3:20): PASTE-YOUTUBE-URL-HERE If you wire MCP servers into an agent, point scan --mcp at your own config and look at what the arrangement can do. The routes are modelled and bounded, the guard is a demo — and the receipt is still a count of zero. Build note: this project was built with AI coding assistance. The repository carries an AI_DISCLOSURE.md describing exactly where and how; every number above traces to a committed file.

title: BlastShield AI: an evidence-first incident commander built on FalkorDB
author: Rohit
summary: The safest cloud response starts with a path, not a prompt BlastShield AI: an evidence-first incident commander built on FalkorDB When a cloud incident starts, the first instinct is usually to find the red service and restart it. That is often too late, too broad, or simply wrong. A compromised Kubernetes pod may be connected to an authentication service. That service may assume an IAM role. The role may read a secret. The secret may unlock a database. The database may replicate into another environment. The visible failure is one node. The real incident is the path behind it. We built BlastShield AI for the Graph Hacks challenge by WeMakeDevs and FalkorDB to answer a more useful question: Given a compromised node, what can it reach, where can we contain it, and what evidence supports that decision? BlastShield stores a synthetic cloud-infrastructure topology in FalkorDB, gives an AI incident commander named KIMO controlled tools to inspect that graph, and requires explicit human approval before any remediation mutation is applied. Live demo: blast-shield-ai.vercel.app Source code: github.com/sandman-sh/BlastShield-AI Contents The problem The idea: walk from the incident to the containment point How a containment candidate is selected What the demo measured Fixing it safely Seeing the graph What we learned What is not done yet If you keep one thing Sources The problem Most incident tools are very good at answering: Which service is returning errors? Which container is using too much CPU? Which deployment happened most recently? Which log line contains the exception? They are less good at answering: What can this compromised component reach? Which relationship makes the incident dangerous? Which node can be isolated without taking down everything else? What remains reachable after containment? That gap matters because cloud infrastructure is connected. A dashboard may show that pod-auth-x92 is compromised. It does not automatically show whether the pod can reach an IAM role, which can read a JWT secret, which can reach the users database. An LLM-only incident assistant has a different problem. It can summarize an incident fluently, but it may invent a dependency, use stale context, or recommend an action without proving the path behind it. BlastShield was designed around a simple rule: The model can explain the decision, but the graph must provide the evidence. The idea: walk from the incident to the containment point BlastShield models infrastructure as a typed property graph in FalkorDB. The graph contains entities such as: APIGateway LoadBalancer K8sPod Service Database IAMRole Secret The relationships are operationally meaningful: CALLS CONNECTS_TO ASSUMES PERMITS READS_SECRET HOSTS REPLICATES_TO This lets the application distinguish a service call from an authorization edge or a secret access path. The incident pipeline is: Incident source → FalkorDB multi-hop traversal → Candidate articulation points → Reachability comparison → Human-readable recommendation → Explicit approval → FalkorDB mutation → Audit record and agent memory The core traversal is executed against FalkorDB through the Redis protocol using GRAPH.QUERY . MATCH path = ( source { id: $sourceNodeId }) - [ * 1 .. 6 ] -> ( downstream ) RETURN downstream , length ( path ) AS hops ORDER BY hops ASC The returned paths become evidence for the incident report. They are not replaced by a generated explanation. How a containment candidate is selected BlastShield does not use a fixed rule such as: If a pod is compromised, shut down the pod. Instead, it combines several pieces of graph evidence. 1. Find downstream impact The system traverses outward from the incident source and records the reachable downstream entities and the number of hops to each one. For example: pod-auth-x92 └── HOSTS → auth-service └── ASSUMES → iam-auth-token └── READS_SECRET → sec-jwt-private └── CONNECTS_TO → users-db 2. Find articulation points BlastShield retrieves the current topology and runs Tarjan's articulation-point algorithm. An articulation point is a node whose removal disconnects part of a graph. In a cloud topology, that can represent a choke point where isolation may stop a cascade without disabling unrelated infrastructure. 3. Compare reachability before and after isolation For each selected candidate, BlastShield measures: Reachable nodes before containment Reachable nodes after candidate isolation Remaining reachable Tier-1 paths This turns a vague recommendation into a measurable trade-off. The system can explain not only what it wants to isolate, but also what the graph predicts will remain available. 4. Let KIMO explain the evidence KIMO is the tool-calling AI incident commander inside BlastShield. The model does not independently calculate the topology. It calls application tools that read FalkorDB and return structured results. The main tools are: inspect_topology analyze_blast_radius recall_memory propose_remediation apply_remediation reset_topology KIMO is instructed to use tools before making claims about nodes, counts, paths, or safety. The language model writes the explanation after the graph analysis has already produced the evidence. What the demo measured The current demo uses a deterministic synthetic infrastructure graph. It is designed to be reproducible and safe for a hackathon demonstration. After seeding the graph, the baseline topology contains: 21 infrastructure nodes 24 relationships Services, databases, pods, IAM roles, and secrets For the demonstration incident, pod-auth-x92 was treated as the compromised source. The live analysis produced: 2 impacted downstream entities 2 hops of downstream impact 2 candidate articulation points in the current topology 19 ingress-reachable nodes before isolation 17 ingress-reachable nodes after the selected cut 13 reachable Tier-1 paths protected after the analysis These are results from the deterministic demo topology, not a production benchmark. The purpose of the scenario is to show that the graph is performing the analysis and that the remediation decision is based on the current topology. The important result is not a universal number. The important result is that the system can show the path, calculate the candidate cut, compare the graph before and after isolation, and preserve the decision as an audit record. Fixing it safely An incident assistant should not turn a conversational sentence into an uncontrolled mutation. BlastShield separates planning from execution. When the operator asks for an analysis, KIMO can inspect the graph and propose a remediation. The proposal does not mutate FalkorDB. The operator must explicitly approve it before apply_remediation is allowed to run. sequenceDiagram participant Operator participant KIMO participant FalkorDB participant Audit Operator->>KIMO: Analyze compromised node KIMO->>FalkorDB: Inspect topology FalkorDB-->>KIMO: Nodes and relationships KIMO->>FalkorDB: Traverse blast radius FalkorDB-->>KIMO: Impact paths KIMO->>KIMO: Run articulation analysis KIMO-->>Operator: Explain and propose Operator->>KIMO: Explicitly approve KIMO->>FalkorDB: Quarantine and mutate graph FalkorDB->>Audit: Persist action hash and memory Audit-->>Operator: Show result The remediation flow can: Quarantine the selected node Sever dangerous permission relationships Select a healthy database candidate for failover Persist a SHA-256 audit hash Store an episodic memory for KIMO Return the new graph state to the console The safety boundary is: AI proposes Human approves Graph mutates The current project simulates infrastructure changes inside the FalkorDB topology. It does not claim to directly modify a user's AWS account or Kubernetes cluster. Seeing the graph The first useful UI decision was to make the topology visible without making the operator understand the database internals first. The command console exposes: FalkorDB connection status Node and edge counts The visual topology Incident selection Blast-radius results KIMO's evidence summary Cypher query execution Approval-gated remediation Audit history Agent memory The command console brings the live graph, incident controls, and agent conversation into one view. The graph is also useful because it gives the operator something to challenge. If KIMO says a database is at risk, the operator can inspect the highlighted path and see which relationships connect the source node to that database. The highlighted path shows why a downstream entity was included in the blast-radius report. The audit view closes the loop. The proposed action is visible before approval, and the resulting mutation is recorded afterward. Memory that stays connected Incident memory is more useful when it keeps its topology context. BlastShield stores AgentMemory nodes in FalkorDB with information such as: Incident category Source node Learned containment strategy Confidence Success rate Timestamp Related audit hash That gives KIMO a path from a previous incident to the action that was taken: graph LR I[Incident] --> S[Source Pod] I --> M[Agent Memory] M --> A[Remediation Action] A --> H[Audit Hash] S --> T[Current Topology] The long-term question is not only: What happened? It is also: What did we do? Did it preserve the right paths? What should we consider next time? What we learned The graph was the product, not the decoration At first, it is tempting to build a graph because graphs look impressive in a demo. That is not enough. The graph became valuable only when every important feature depended on it: Blast-radius analysis reads graph paths. Cut-vertex analysis reads graph structure. Remediation mutates graph state. Audit records are stored in the graph. Agent memory is stored in the graph. If the graph is removed, the main product behavior disappears. Deterministic analysis should come before fluent explanation We learned to keep the language model away from the parts that should be reproducible. The graph traversal, articulation-point analysis, reachability calculation, and mutation rules are application logic. KIMO's job is to choose the appropriate tool, summarize the result, explain the evidence, and ask for approval. The safest action may be smaller than the obvious action The obvious response to a compromised pod is often to disable the whole service. The graph can reveal a smaller containment point that breaks the dangerous path while preserving more healthy connectivity. That is the difference between reacting to a red node and reasoning about a connected system. Approval is not the opposite of autonomy An autonomous agent can investigate independently and prepare a high-quality action plan without silently changing production state. The approval gate made the system more trustworthy because the operator can inspect the evidence before the mutation occurs. Synthetic data can still demonstrate real architecture We used synthetic infrastructure data so the demo is public, reproducible, and safe. That does not make the graph behavior fake. The topology, queries, traversal, analysis, mutation, audit, and memory flows are real application behavior. It does mean we are careful not to claim that this version is already a production AWS or Kubernetes controller. What is not done yet There are important limitations. No live cloud ingestion yet The current graph is seeded from a deterministic synthetic topology. The next version should ingest authorized data from Kubernetes, AWS IAM, cloud databases, service meshes, and deployment systems. Remediation is graph-level simulation The current remediation changes the FalkorDB representation and records the action. It does not execute kubectl , AWS SDK calls, or cloud-provider mutations. That is appropriate for the hackathon demo, but a production version would need provider-specific connectors, permissions, rollback, and policy enforcement. No production multi-tenancy yet A real SaaS version would require tenant isolation, role-based access control, secret rotation, encrypted connections, per-project credentials, and a detailed authorization model. The demo is not a benchmark The numbers in this post come from the deterministic demo scenario. We have not presented them as a general production accuracy benchmark. That distinction matters because trustworthy incident tooling should report what it has measured, not what sounds impressive. If you keep one thing The safest incident response starts with a path, not a prompt. The path tells you what the compromised component can reach. The graph tells you where a cut may contain the incident. The algorithm compares the consequences. The agent explains the evidence. The human approves the change. That is the design behind BlastShield AI. Technology BlastShield AI uses: FalkorDB Next.js TypeScript React OpenCypher Redis wire protocol OpenRouter-compatible AI APIs Tarjan articulation-point analysis SHA-256 audit hashes Docker Compose Vercel Sources BlastShield AI source repository BlastShield AI live demo FalkorDB AI Assistance Disclosure AI coding assistants were used for implementation assistance, debugging, documentation, and testing support. The project team reviewed, tested, and understands the submitted code, graph model, queries, architecture, security boundaries, and product decisions.

title: Why Vector RAG Fails AI Agents: Building an Autonomous SRE Swarm with FalkorDB
author: SidakSethi-Singh
summary: Large Language Models depend on the context they are given. In the year the usual way to give context has been Vector RAG (embeddings plus cosine similarity).. In real production settings especially for enterprise microservices and site reliability engineering Vector RAG fails completely . When an incident hits a distributed system an AI agent does not need text similarity. It must know: What breaks three hops if this database goes down? Which recent code. Pull request touched this service’s connection pool? What past incident had this exact failure signature. How was it resolved? Who owns this service. Who is on call right now? Embeddings cannot answer multi‑hop causal questions. Graphs can. That is why we created FalkorSynapse for the WeMakeDevs Graph Hacks 2026 Hackathon . Why FalkorDB? Solving the Latency Bottleneck graph databases such as Neo4j use pointer‑chasing traversal algorithms. These are powerful for batch queries. They are too slow to run inside an AI agent’s active step‑by‑step reasoning loop. FalkorDB is different. It represents graphs as ** adjacency matrices powered by GraphBLAS linear algebra in C* . Multi‑hop traversals and graph algorithms do not walk pointers; they perform matrix multiplications in **sub‑milliseconds (<1 ms) *. This architectural breakthrough let us make FalkorDB the active central nervous system of a multi‑agent swarm. The Architecture: 3 Agents, 1 Synaptic Mesh FalkorSynapse models an enterprise FinTech platform (Services, PostgreSQL, Kafka, Redis, Engineers, Pull Requests and Incident Runbooks) as a graph orchestrated by three specialized agents: 1. The Topology Sentinel (Track 01: Acting on Connected Data) When an anomaly appears the Topology Sentinel runs OpenCypher traversals to calculate the downstream blast radius across multiple hops: MATCH path = ( root { id: $target_id }) - [ :ROUTES_THROUGH | FORWARD_CALL | PUBLISHES_EVENT | WRITES_TRANSACTIONS * 1 .. 3 ] -> ( downstream ) RETURN downstream.id , downstream.name , length ( path ) as depth ORDER , BY depth ASC ; It calls FalkorDB 's native PageRank algorithm to determine system vulnerability and correlates recent git deployments to identify the root cause. 2. The Episodic Memory Coordinator (Track 02: Agent Memory) Instead of dumping chat transcripts into an LLM context window, FalkorSynapse stores episodic incident graphs (:PastIncident) and validated procedural runbooks (:Runbook) in FalkorDB. When an alert fires, it recalls how past failures were resolved, fetches the highest-confidence automated runbook, and coordinates inter-agent state handoffs via immutable graph tokens (:AgentHandoff). 3. The Enterprise Brain (Track 03: Company Brain) Institutional knowledge is usually fragmented across Slack channels and stale docs. FalkorSynapse maps structural ownership: cypher MATCH (e:Engineer)-[r:PRIMARY_ARCHITECT|SCHEMA_OWNER|MAINTAINER]->(target {id: $target_id}) RETURN e.name, e.role, e.slack, e.on_call, type(r) AS relation; It instantly identifies the system architect, checks the active on-call rotation, and correlates git author provenance. Autonomous Healing in Action With one click, FalkorSynapse executes the verified runbook, updates the live graph back to healthy, and writes the mitigation into FalkorDB' s persistent memory. The swarm actually learns from every incident. Engineers can also talk directly to the architecture using our GraphRAG Natural Language Agent — translating plain English questions like "Who owns Payments Core and who is on call?" into OpenCypher queries executed in under 0.1 ms. Key Takeaways Context is not decoration: If you remove the graph database from an agentic system and the system still works , you built a toy. In FalkorSynapse , FalkorDB is the engine. GraphBLAS changes the game: Sub - millisecond graph queries make it possible to run graph algorithms inside the inner reasoning loop of AI agents without latency penalties. The future of SRE is graph - native: Connecting code commits , services , teams , and runbooks into a single graph is the only way autonomous agents can reason safely in production. title: Nine people know this part of Kubernetes. It still depends on one.
author: Balaji Thukuntala
summary: Every team has that one person. Every review waits for them, and when they say "I'll be offline next week", three people quietly panic. For Graph Hacks (WeMakeDevs x FalkorDB) I built something that finds these people in Kubernetes. It's called Understudy. Here's the story, mostly in memes. Every team has this moment The lie we tell ourselves This is a real part of Kubernetes, pkg/kubelet/apis/config . Nine people know the code. Six people can approve changes. Sounds safe. Except every single path between those two groups goes through one person. So I stopped counting people Understudy counts routes instead: someone who knows the code, connected to someone who can approve it, with nobody shared between routes. That count is the "understudy number". Here it's 1. FalkorDB does the counting with a built-in algorithm called max-flow, so it's an actual measurement, not a vibe. Meet contributor-25b5f Everyone shows up as a pseudonym, so I don't know who this is. I just know they should never take a vacation. So I rehearsed them leaving Understudy copies the whole graph, takes them off the copy, and checks what breaks. 41 of 79 parts of Kubernetes get weaker. The real data never changes. It also suggests the cheapest fix. Here, pairing one person who knows the code with one approver is enough to get a backup. I added an AI agent. It's humble. You can ask it questions in plain English. It can only answer from the graph, so when something isn't there, it presses the second button. Every answer also shows the queries it ran. Then I argued with it Every answer gets fact-checked against the graph before you see it. Here the agent was right, and the check was also right. I fixed it by making the tools say things in plain words, so the agent can quote them. FalkorDB and I had one small disagreement I tested every number against networkx. With mixed capacities, max-flow came out low on 8 of 150 test graphs. With every capacity set to 1, they agreed every time. So everything is 1 now. Problem solved by not having the problem. OK but does it actually work? I checked it against real people who left Kubernetes. Only 7 of 39 cases had enough data, and none of them hit a 1. So honestly, I can't prove it yet. The whole result, including what didn't work, is in the app anyway. Try it It runs on a free server with a tenth of a CPU. Getting it to start in 30 seconds instead of 2 minutes was its own adventure. Live app: https://understudy-u2qk.onrender.com BalajiReddy1 / understudy My Graph Hacks entry. Models Kubernetes as a company in FalkorDB and checks who could actually step in if someone left. Understudy Understudy measures how many people a team can lose before nobody who approves changes to a system can reach anyone who knows its code. It models Kubernetes as a graph in FalkorDB, computes that number for every part of the codebase with max-flow, lets you rehearse a departure on a copy of the graph, and includes an agent that answers questions only from graph queries and shows every query it ran. Live app: https://understudy-u2qk.onrender.com Built for Graph Hacks: Context for AI Agents (WeMakeDevs x FalkorDB), October 2026. Tracks: Company Brain, and Agents That Act on Connected Data.
